results.title: Reproducibility over platforms - PyTorch Forums
results.content:
Title: Reproducibility over platforms - PyTorch Forums
# Reproducibility over platforms. Unfortunately, my model is not reproducible even when ran in Docker containers on two different platforms. It is of course reproducible on the same platform. What is the reason for the non-deterministic behavior over different platforms? Currently, you seem to ask “can I run my stuff anywhere and expect it to be reproducible” and the answer is just “no”. The first step to a more detailed answer would be to narrow the problem by a lot. “I want to do X and I have platforms that are exactly identical except for Y.” could be something that could be worked on. (Note, though, that the general interest seems to be mostly in having reproducibility in the sense of non-random behavior rather than implementing it.). In the end, the crux is that floating point operations don’t commute (nor does the distributive property work out exactly).Then crux is that things are not guaranteed to run in the exact same order e.g. on different hardware because the difference in hardware might actually mean that things are translated to different GPU kernels or some such. I am trying to reproduce a simple MNIST example on the CPU (later GPU, but that’s a different topic) with the exact same loss on two machines. However, BOTH machines are pretty much naked and running everything inside a Docker container, which sets up the whole environment. I fixed all possible seeds and get reproducible results on the respective machines, but NOT BETWEEN the machines. To summarize: the platforms share everything except for the hardware (CPU, RAM, Mainboard). (I may ask the same thing again with GPUs, which make the problem more difficult, but this post focuses on the CPU). If researchers want to reproduce any of my findings, they should be able to at least reproduce the CPU result on their platform, no? I don’t think reproducibility in terms of “exact same floating point number” is reasonably achievable, e.g. AVX vs. non-AVX will make a difference. If your reproducibility depends on floating point accuracy divergences (sadly a lot of DL stuff does), something bad is going on, anyways.

results.title: Datalad Reproducibility for High Performance Computing: The Datalad Slurm Extension · distribits
results.content: 3. Datalad Reproducibility for High Performance Computing: The Datalad Slurm Extension/. # Datalad Reproducibility for High Performance Computing: The Datalad Slurm Extension. Talk Andreas Knüpfer Distribits 2025 HdU plenary hall Datalad Other Research data management Computing Data-Science Reproducibility. Datalad run and rerun are incompatible with HPC. The talk presents how we fixed it. Datalad run and rerun for machine-actionable reproducibility is not working in High Performance Computing (HPC) environments where compute jobs are managed through a batch scheduling system. Using datalad run outside of Slurm for job submission is pointless. We present the Datalad Slurm extension to solve this for the Slurm batch scheduling system. They allow to schedule many jobs at the same time from the same clone of a repository and generate a reproducibility record in the git log for successful jobs. The talk introduces the solution from the user perspective, explains the design idea and some implementation details, presents some performance evaluation, and touches a few extra features.

results.title: Seeding and reproducibility of random numbers - NumPy
results.content: Seeding and reproducibility of random numbers - NumPy Seeding and Reproducibility of Random Numbers in NumPy Random numbers play a significant role in various scientific fields, statistical simulations, and machine learning algorithms. NumPy, a fundamental package for scientific computing in Python, provides a versatile set of functions to generate random numbers. In this article, we will explore the concept of seeding and reproducibility of random numbers in NumPy. Understanding Randomness in NumPy Random numbers generated by a computer are not truly random but are referred to as pseudo-random numbers. NumPy uses various algorithms to generate pseudo-random numbers, including the Mersenne Twister algorithm. The random number generation process begins with an initial seed value, which is used as a starting point by the pseudo-random number generator. Seeding the Random Number Generator Seeding the random number generator allows us to specify the initial state, or the seed, for the algorithm. This seed value determines the sequence of random numbers generated. By setting the same seed, we can obtain the same sequence of random numbers consistently. Here is an example of setting the seed and generating a sequence of random numbers: Output: `[0.37454012 0.95071431 0.73199394 0.59865848 0.15601864]` In this example, we set the seed to 42 before generating a sequence of five uniform random numbers between 0 and 1. By setting the seed at the beginning of the code, you ensure that every user running the code will obtain the same set of random numbers. The generated random numbers within a single program run will be identical, but the numbers might differ across different versions of NumPy or on different machines due to algorithmic changes or hardware variations. These functions might have their own random number generators, and setting the seed in NumPy won't affect them. To ensure complete reproducibility, all random number generators in use should be seeded properly. Ensuring reproducibility of random numbers is crucial in scientific computing and statistical simulations. NumPy provides an elegant solution through its seed function, allowing us to generate the same sequence of random numbers consistently. With NumPy, you can confidently incorporate random numbers into your projects, knowing that your results can be easily reproduced and validated.
